line: A traveling folk-pop songwriter, fresh off a year of Oregon dates.
intro: A.C. Sapphire started playing out at the end of 2019 and has hardly stopped moving since.
story: Her records came two years apart, Desert Car in 2022 and December 32nd in 2024, the second named for a day that only exists when the calendar runs out. She came to Pickathon in 2026 for a Saturday evening at the Farmhouse, between a year of Oregon dates and sessions for a new album in North Carolina. She is rarely in one place for long.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 6 pm, Farmhouse

line: San Francisco heavy-psych pioneers, three decades of riffs behind them, in 2026.
intro: In 1993 Lori S. started a band in San Francisco that went the other way from everyone else: slower, heavier, louder. Thirty years on, it still does.
story:
She played guitar and sang, with Joey Osbourne on drums and Peter Lucas on bass. Zoroaster came out on Sympathy for the Record Industry in 1995, and Busse Woods followed in 1999 on Man's Ruin, the label at the center of the early stoner-rock scene. By 2003 the reference books, The Encyclopedia of Heavy Metal among them, were writing Acid King in as pioneers of the sound.

They never hurried. III arrived in 2005, then ten quiet years, then Middle of Nowhere, Center of Everywhere in 2015 and Beyond Vision on Blues Funeral in 2023, each built on the same patient riff. In 2026 they played Pickathon three times, from a late Friday in the Woods to a Sunday afternoon in the Galaxy Barn, and by October they were planning a 2027 tour of Latin America. Still slow, still heavy.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 11 pm, Woods · Sat Aug 1, 6 pm, Slab · Sun Aug 2, 1 pm, Galaxy Barn

line: Her sixth Pickathon, nineteen years after the first, with Who's Keeping Time? in hand.
intro: Alela Diane put out her first records herself, from a small town in the California foothills. More than twenty years later, she made her seventh in her own attic.
story:
She grew up in Nevada City, California, singing with her musician parents, and self-released The Pirate's Gospel in 2004. When Portland's Holocene label reissued it in 2006, The Times and NME took notice, and Rough Trade signed her. To Be Still followed in 2009; Uncut called it a quantum leap. She played Glastonbury and Primavera Sound that summer, sang on Later... with Jools Holland, and opened for Fleet Foxes in America and Europe.

Then life came into the songs. Cusp, in 2018, took its title from nearly dying in childbirth and what she understood afterward, and it carried her through a run of theaters in Britain, France and the Netherlands. In May 2026 came Who's Keeping Time?, recorded live over five days in the attic of her Victorian house, and it made Mojo's list of the year's albums. That summer she played Pickathon for the sixth time, nineteen years after the first, with three sets in two days, then toured Britain, Ireland and Europe in the fall. The girl from Nevada City is still making records at home.
sets: Thu Jul 30, 5 pm, Cherry Hill · Thu Jul 30, 9 pm, Edge · Fri Jul 31, 11 am, Windmill

line: A Penrose Records find in 2023. Three years on, they returned as a Daptone band.
intro: The Altons came out of Southeast Los Angeles playing sweet, heartbroken soul. In 2023 they were on Daptone's little sister label; by 2025 they were on Daptone itself.
story: The band started playing out in 2015 and put out its first music in 2020. Penrose Records, the Daptone imprint for Southern California's soul revival, took them on, and in 2023 they played Austin City Limits. Heartache in Room 14, their debut album, came out on Daptone in February 2025; a month later they sang "Float" on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert, and their first national tour took them to Bonnaroo, Chicago's Thalia Hall and London's Jazz Café. In 2026 they came back to Pickathon, three years after their first visit, for a Sunday afternoon set in the Woods. Same sweet soul, a bigger name on the label.
sets: Sun Aug 2, 3 pm, Woods

line: Four years on, a Stones Throw band, still playing post-punk with no guitars.
intro: Automatic play post-punk with no guitars at all: drums, bass, synthesizer and three voices. It was enough to get them signed to Stones Throw two years after they started.
story:
Izzy Glaudini, Halle Saxon and Lola Dompé formed the band in Los Angeles in 2017. Dompé's father, Kevin Haskins, had drummed in Bauhaus; a few years later his daughter's band would open for his old one at the Greek Theatre. Stones Throw signed them in June 2019, Signal came out that fall, and Pitchfork heard a band that would have been at home in the late '70s. Excess followed in 2022, along with Primavera Sound.

Is It Now?, their third album, arrived in September 2025 and landed on Under the Radar's year-end list. The next summer they came back to Pickathon, four years after their first visit, for an evening in the Woods and a midnight slot on the Paddock. There are still no guitars, and nobody misses them.
sets: Thu Jul 30, midnight, Paddock · Fri Jul 31, 7 pm, Woods

line: A Portland storyteller of unhurried Americana, playing his hometown festival in 2026.
intro: Barna Howard writes plainspoken Americana and has never been in a hurry about it.
story: Portland's Mama Bird Recording Co. put out his self-titled debut in 2012 and Quite a Feelin' in 2015, songs that take their time getting where they're going. In 2026 he played a Saturday afternoon set at Pickathon's Farmhouse, close to home. You are still most likely to find him on a weeknight at the Laurelthirst.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 1 pm, Farmhouse

line: Georgia-born, soulful Southern country, new to the farm in 2026.
intro: Ben Chapman is a Georgia-born country singer who made Nashville his base.
story: He spent 2026 touring behind his album Feet on Fire, with three Pickathon sets in two days along the way, and he keeps a gathering of his own going in Nashville every year: the Peach Jam.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 9 pm, Cherry Hill · Sun Aug 2, noon, Pumphouse · Sun Aug 2, 3 pm, Galaxy Barn

line: Winnipeg's J.J. Cale-style country folk, Americana's emerging act nominee.
intro: Boy Golden plays Winnipeg country at the speed of a long summer afternoon. In five years it took him from a first record to Nashville's list of emerging acts.
story:
Liam Duncan, from Brandon, Manitoba, took the name from his mother's maiden name, Golden, and started the project in 2021: a laid-back country-folk sound that owes more to J.J. Cale than to Music Row, and Six Shooter Records put it out. The albums came quickly. For Jimmy won Contemporary Album of the Year at the Canadian Folk Music Awards, and For Eden was nominated for a Juno in 2025.

Best of Our Possible Lives arrived in February 2026 and made the Polaris Music Prize long list, and the Americana Music Association named him a nominee for Emerging Act of the Year. That summer he played Pickathon twice, once in the Galaxy Barn after 1 a.m., and in the fall he put out a deluxe edition and booked a headline tour of Canada. Still unhurried, and suddenly everywhere.
sets: Thu Jul 30, late night (1 am), Galaxy Barn · Fri Jul 31, 9 pm, Cherry Hill

line: A Texas duo on ATO Records, on the farm in 2026 with Heat of July.
intro: Briscoe is two voices from Texas in close harmony. Two years after their first record, they were opening for Noah Kahan and Zach Bryan.
story: The duo put out their first music in 2021, and ATO Records released West of It All in 2023. That September they played the Gorge Amphitheatre, and Dave Matthews gave them a shout-out from the stage; Bonnaroo came the same year, Lollapalooza and Newport Folk the next. Heat of July followed in September 2025, along with the first weekend of Austin City Limits. In 2026 they played a late Friday afternoon set at Pickathon's Cherry Hill, then spent the fall on the road with Phillip Phillips. Two voices, still in harmony.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 5 pm, Cherry Hill

line: Eleven years after their first farm set, Bay Area string-band fun again.
intro: The Brothers Comatose are a San Francisco string band built around two actual brothers, Ben and Alex Morrison, and a van that has seen a lot of the country.
story: They started in 2008 and called their second album, in 2012, Respect the Van. A string band in a rock town, they found their crowd at Hardly Strictly Bluegrass, High Sierra and Outside Lands, and headlined the Kate Wolf Music Festival. The records kept coming every few years, City Painted Gold, Ink, Dust & Luck, Turning Up the Ground and, in 2025, Golden Grass. Eleven years after their first visit, they came back to Pickathon in 2026 and played a little of everything: the Edge, a Thursday night on the Paddock, the Woods, and a dinner set at Curation with Cafe Olli. The brothers are still in the van.
sets: Thu Jul 30, 7 pm, Edge · Thu Jul 30, 10 pm, Paddock · Fri Jul 31, 6:30 pm, Curation (dinner with Cafe Olli) · Fri Jul 31, 9 pm, Woods

line: Portland art punks with a taste for theater.
intro: Buddy Wynkoop came together in Portland during the pandemic, an art-punk band with a taste for theater.
story: They played Pickathon three times in 2026, from the Grove at noon to the Galaxy Barn late on Sunday, and spent that year sharing a split EP, Crippling Fun, with the Portland band Nug while they worked on a second album for 2027.
sets: Sat Aug 1, noon, Grove · Sat Aug 1, 1:30 pm, Slab · Sun Aug 2, 11 pm, Galaxy Barn

line: Boise's guitar heroes, back on the farm in 2026, more than thirty years into the band.
intro: Doug Martsch started Built to Spill in Boise in 1992 with the idea that the band could change around him. More than thirty years later, it still does.
story:
Boise was a long way from indie rock's capitals, and Martsch's long, tangled guitar songs made it matter anyway. Warner Bros. signed the band in 1995, and the records they made there and just before, There's Nothing Wrong with Love, Perfect from Now On and Keep It Like a Secret, all landed in the top fifty of Pitchfork's list of the best albums of the 1990s.

The Warner run lasted twenty years. In April 2022 Martsch signed to Sub Pop, the label he said he had wanted to join since he was a teenager, and that September came When the Wind Forgets Your Name, their first album of new songs in seven years, made with bassist Melanie Radford and drummer Teresa Esguerra; Mojo called the band "one of the States' great indie rock institutions". They toured with Yo La Tengo in 2025 and came back to Pickathon in 2026 for a third time, with a Saturday night at Cherry Hill and a Sunday night on the Paddock. The lineup has changed again; the guitar is still unmistakably his.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 11 pm, Cherry Hill · Sun Aug 2, 10 pm, Paddock

line: A honky-tonk songwriter whose songs other country singers record.
intro: Channing Wilson played honky-tonks for more than fifteen years before he put out a record of his own.
story: Dead Man arrived in 2023. In 2026 he played Pickathon three times in two days, and by the fall one of his songs was on the soundtrack of Heartland and a new album, I Ain't No Outlaw, was in the works with Dave Cobb producing. The long road in is finally paying out.
sets: Thu Jul 30, 5 pm, Pumphouse · Thu Jul 30, 11 pm, Galaxy Barn · Fri Jul 31, 6 pm, Paddock

line: Former bassist of the Gladiators and a roots-reggae elder of Seattle, in 2026.
intro: Clinton Fearon learned reggae from the inside, playing bass at Studio One and the Black Ark when the music was young. Then he came to Seattle on tour and stayed.
story:
For eighteen years, from 1969 to 1987, he was the bassist and one of the singers in The Gladiators, and he co-wrote two of their best-known songs, "Chatty Chatty Mouth" and "Richman Poorman." Between Gladiators records he played sessions at two of the studios that shaped Jamaican music, Coxsone Dodd's Studio One and Lee Perry's Black Ark.

When the Gladiators finished their last American tour in 1987, he and a few bandmates used the time left on their visas to start a band in Seattle, and he never went back; his first solo album came out in 1994. Three decades later he was still writing: Jah Is Love, made with the French band Riddim Source, came out in June 2025. In 2026 he played Pickathon on a Saturday evening at Cherry Hill and again that night at the Edge, and 2026 also brought a new single, "To Remember." Almost forty years on, Seattle still has its reggae elder.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 7 pm, Cherry Hill · Sat Aug 1, 9 pm, Edge

line: Portland spiritual jazz of horns and cello, meditative and warm.
intro: The Cosmic Tones Research Trio make slow, spiritual jazz in Portland, on horn, cello and keys.
story: Roman Norfleet, Harlan Silverman and Kennedy Verrett put out their first record in 2024. Their second, a self-titled LP, came out on Portland's Mississippi Records in October 2025 and traveled farther than local jazz usually does: Rough Trade stocked it, so did shops in Germany and Canada, and Aquarium Drunkard brought the trio onto its Transmissions podcast. In 2026 they opened their Pickathon weekend on a Friday morning in the Woods. Quiet music, finding its listeners a long way from home.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 11 am, Woods · Fri Jul 31, 1:30 pm, Pumphouse · Sun Aug 2, noon, Lucky Barn

line: A Louisiana bluesman in B.B. King's line, now on Alligator Records.
intro: D.K. Harrell plays the blues the way B.B. King did: clean, singing guitar lines and a voice that fills a room. He is a young man playing an old style, and the blues world noticed fast.
story:
He came out of Louisiana, and his first album, The Right Man, came out on the nonprofit Little Village Foundation. The Blues Music Awards put it up for Best Emerging Artist Album in 2024, and Living Blues magazine's critics honored it in their poll that year.

In March 2025 Alligator Records, the Chicago label that has been home to the blues since 1971, signed him. Talkin' Heavy, produced by Kid Andersen, followed, and the Blues Music Awards nominated it for Album of the Year in 2026. That summer he played Pickathon three times, from the Lucky Barn on Saturday evening to a Sunday afternoon in the Woods. The old style has a young voice again.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 6 pm, Lucky Barn · Sat Aug 1, 11 pm, Edge · Sun Aug 2, 1 pm, Woods

line: Irish tradition on resonator guitar and banjo, with a Claddagh debut, on the farm in 2026.
intro: DUG built a following in Dublin's clubs before they had released a single song.
story: Conor O'Reilly and Jonny Pickett started the duo in 2023, resonator guitar and banjo, Irish tradition played with an American old-time drive. Word of mouth did the rest: by early 2024 they were playing Whelan's, and Claddagh Records, the label behind The Chieftains, put out their debut, Have At It!, in September 2025. In 2026 they crossed the Atlantic for two Pickathon sets, in the Galaxy Barn and the Lucky Barn. The crowd came first; now there's a record to go with it.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 1 pm, Galaxy Barn · Sun Aug 2, 6 pm, Lucky Barn

line: An Arkansas honky-tonk songwriter, wry and open-hearted.
intro: Dylan Earl writes Arkansas country, honky-tonk with a wink and a lot of heart for the people who raised him.
story: He put out his first record in 2017, and by 2023's I Saw the Arkansas, Paste was putting him on its list of the year's best country, folk and Americana. Level-Headed Even Smile followed in September 2025 on Gar Hole Records, with Willi Carlisle and Jess Harp as guests, a record that looks back at the small-town mentors who shaped him. In 2026 he played Pickathon on Saturday evening in the Woods and Sunday evening in the Galaxy Barn. Every song still has an Arkansas address.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 7 pm, Woods · Sun Aug 2, 7 pm, Galaxy Barn

line: Yemeni melodies on instruments welded from scrap metal, led by Eyal El Wahab.
intro: Eyal El Wahab builds his band's instruments out of scrap metal and junk, then plays Yemeni songs on them.
story: His family's music came from Yemen; his band came together in Tel Aviv, and its first album, Saadia Jefferson, arrived in 2019. Albat Alawi Op.99 followed in 2022 and Mute, on the German label Glitterbeat, in 2024; PopMatters ranked it eighth among the year's global albums and called El Khat's music "unlike anyone else's." In 2026 the band played Pickathon three times, the last of them after midnight on the Paddock as Sunday turned into Monday, and went back to work on a fourth album. Whatever is lying around, still turned into music.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 7 pm, Galaxy Barn · Sun Aug 2, 9 pm, Edge · Sun Aug 2, midnight, Paddock

line: A Santa Fe songwriter of candid, hook-filled country rock.
intro: Esther Rose grew up in Michigan, learned country music in New Orleans and kept writing it after she moved to New Mexico.
story: She put out her first album, This Time Last Night, in 2017, and How Many Times, in 2021, was the one that traveled: Mojo heard a writer who looks for lessons rather than burned bridges, and Uncut and PopMatters agreed. Then she traded New Orleans for Taos, and Safe to Run, her first record for New West, in 2023, was the chronicle of that move; it was nominated for a Libera Award. Want, her fifth album, followed in May 2025 to warm reviews in Mojo and Uncut. In 2026 she played Pickathon twice, from a Saturday morning at the Windmill to a Sunday evening on the Paddock. Three states in, and she still writes every one of them down.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 11 am, Windmill · Sun Aug 2, 6 pm, Paddock

line: A Rio-born guitarist of seven-string Brazilian jazz, in Los Angeles.
intro: Fabiano do Nascimento grew up in Rio de Janeiro playing the seven-string guitar, the instrument that carries the bass lines of Brazilian choro.
story: He brought it to Los Angeles, and his first record came out in 2015. PopMatters called his 2017 album, Tempo dos Mestres, monumental, and in 2020 he played NPR's Tiny Desk. The Room, his 2024 duo record with the Los Angeles saxophonist Sam Gendel, drew The Guardian's top rating, and in February 2026 he put out Vila, made with the trombonist Vittor Santos and a sixteen-piece ensemble. That summer he played a single Saturday afternoon set at Pickathon, in the Lucky Barn. Rio's guitar, a long way from Rio, still sounds like home.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 4 pm, Lucky Barn

line: A tight Los Angeles soul collective, all harmonies and pocket grooves, in 2026.
intro: Family Company is a Los Angeles soul collective built on longtime studio friendships, all harmonies and pocket grooves.
story: They started playing out in 2023. In July 2026 they released in & out on their own FamCo Records, and a few weeks later they played Pickathon three times, from a midnight set on the Paddock on Friday to Saturday night in the Woods.
sets: Fri Jul 31, midnight, Paddock · Sat Aug 1, 3 pm, Pumphouse · Sat Aug 1, 9 pm, Woods

line: Two years on, the Philadelphia band came back louder, with a live album to prove it.
intro: Florry began as Francie Medosch's songs and grew into a seven-piece Philadelphia country-rock band that plays like a party.
story:
Medosch's early records came out on small labels, Brown Bunny in 2018 and Big Fall in 2021. The band filled out around her, and when The Holey Bible arrived on Dear Life in 2023, weepy old-school twang with loud guitars, it was Stereogum's Album of the Week and a favorite of Pitchfork and Paste.

Sounds Like..., in May 2025, was looser and louder, part hangout and part guitar solo, and it ended the year near the top of Paste's and BrooklynVegan's lists. Two years after their first visit, they came back to Pickathon in 2026 for three sets, from the Slab to a late Friday at Cherry Hill, and a live record followed, Smells Like... Florry Live As Hell. Still Medosch's songs, just more people playing them.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 3 pm, Slab · Fri Jul 31, 11 pm, Cherry Hill · Sat Aug 1, 5 pm, Galaxy Barn

line: Three Melbourne voices in close harmony, a debut critics loved.
intro: Folk Bitch Trio are three Melbourne singers who sing so close together it can be hard to tell whose voice is whose.
story: They started playing out in 2021, and their debut, Now Would Be a Good Time, came out on Jagjaguwar in July 2025. NME gave it five stars for its "breathtaking vocal harmonies," and Mojo called it an exquisite, arresting introduction. At home it earned four ARIA nominations and, in 2026, three AIR Awards, Breakthrough Independent Artist among them. That summer they played Pickathon three times in two days, and they also made their first trip to Roskilde. Three voices, still hard to tell apart.
sets: Fri Jul 31, noon, Pumphouse · Fri Jul 31, 5 pm, Woods · Sat Aug 1, 5 pm, Cherry Hill

line: Portland post-punk, back in 2026 a year after their first farm set.
intro: Forty Feet Tall have been playing Portland's clubs since 2013, long enough to be a local fixture and still be somebody's new favorite band.
story: Their first record came out in 2014. By 2022 they were playing Treefort in Boise, and the Portland Mercury, previewing a month of local music that January, picked them as a band to fall for. They played Pickathon in 2025, put out Clean the Cage that September and came back the next summer for sets at the Slab and the Galaxy Barn. Thirteen years in, still somebody's new favorite.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 1:30 pm, Slab · Fri Jul 31, 9 pm, Galaxy Barn

line: Dan Wriggins' dry, poetic indie rock with pedal steel, on Merge.
intro: Dan Wriggins writes songs like small, funny poems about ordinary days, and his band Friendship plays them slow, with pedal steel in the corners.
story: The Philadelphia band put out its first record in 2014 and kept at it for eight years before the wider world caught on. Love the Stranger, in 2022, was Stereogum's Album of the Week, and the next summer they played End of the Road in England. Caveman Wakes Up, their first album for Merge, came out in 2025, was Album of the Week again and made Stereogum's list of the year's fifty best. In May 2026 they headlined The Dome in London; that summer they played Pickathon three times, from the Grove to the Lucky Barn, then went back out on a winter tour of American clubs. Ordinary days, still worth writing down.
sets: Fri Jul 31, noon, Grove · Fri Jul 31, 7 pm, Edge · Sat Aug 1, 2 pm, Lucky Barn

line: Fingerpicked folk with soaring vocals. Nested in Tangles was a critics' pick.
intro: Hannah Frances writes knotty, fingerpicked folk that moves like jazz. Her breakthrough came out of the hardest year of her life.
story: The Vermont songwriter put out her first music in 2017 and spent years releasing records on her own. Keeper of the Shepherd, in 2024, was about her father's death; Pitchfork called it dazzling and PopMatters put it fourth among the year's folk albums. Nested in Tangles, her sixth album, came out on Fire Talk in October 2025 and went further, bringing in drums and stranger time; Stereogum made it Album of the Week, and Paste and Treble ranked it among the year's best. In May 2026 she headlined the Old Town School of Folk Music in Chicago, and that summer she played Pickathon at the Windmill and Cherry Hill. Grief, turned into something intricate, still unfolding.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 3 pm, Windmill · Sun Aug 2, 5 pm, Cherry Hill

line: A young songwriter with an online following, playing confessional folk-pop in 2026.
intro: Hannah Hill is a young songwriter who found her first audience online, with candid acoustic songs about heartbreak.
story: She has been playing out since 2022 and kept sharing stripped-down singles, "Lacy" and "Horses Run" among them. In 2026 she played Pickathon twice, in the Galaxy Barn on Friday and the Lucky Barn on Sunday.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 1 pm, Galaxy Barn · Sun Aug 2, 2 pm, Lucky Barn

line: Pure Tennessee classic country, twang and all.
intro: Hannah Juanita sings country music the old way, and makes no apology for it.
story: Her first album, Hardliner, came out in 2021, a title that doubled as a statement of intent. Tennessee Songbird followed in August 2024, and Saving Country Music, which keeps a close eye on the genre's traditionalists, gave it a strong review. In July 2026 she released The Magnolia Sessions, recorded outdoors under a tree in Nashville, and a few weeks later she played Pickathon in the Galaxy Barn and on the Paddock. The old way, out in the open air.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 7 pm, Galaxy Barn · Sat Aug 1, 6 pm, Paddock

line: Rowdy Nashville old-time, on the farm in 2026 after their album Down the Road.
intro: Hogslop String Band have been playing rowdy old-time string music in Nashville since 2011.
story: Their album Down the Road came out in 2025, and in 2026 they brought it to Pickathon for a Friday at the Windmill and a Sunday in the Lucky Barn, then kept the singles coming, a live "Jolene" among them.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 1 pm, Windmill · Sun Aug 2, 4 pm, Lucky Barn

line: Gritty, atmospheric songs, a record named Doom Country, a name to watch.
intro: Hudson Freeman grew up in Eswatini, the son of missionaries, and ended up writing gritty folk songs in Brooklyn.
story: He had been putting out records on his own since 2015, to small audiences, when a rough demo called "If You Know Me" went viral in November 2025. The year that followed moved fast: Newport Folk, three Pickathon sets in late July, at the Slab, the Paddock and the Grove, and the Club stage at Pukkelpop in Belgium in August. In November 2026 Mom+Pop released Doom Country, his first album with a label, and Paste admired its rough, staticky twang; a tour of Europe and North America was booked for 2027. Ten years of records in near-obscurity, then one demo.
sets: Thu Jul 30, 5 pm, Slab · Thu Jul 30, 8 pm, Paddock · Fri Jul 31, 2 pm, Grove

line: Second summer running for the Portland five-piece: quiet horns, then roaring guitars.
intro: Jonny's Day Out is a Portland five-piece that sets quiet horn passages against loud guitars.
story: Willamette Week once had to explain their bunny costume. They played Pickathon in 2025 and came back the next summer with a new single, "Zumba," for three sets across Friday and Saturday, from the Slab to a Saturday morning in the Woods.
sets: Fri Jul 31, noon, Slab · Fri Jul 31, 3 pm, Galaxy Barn · Sat Aug 1, 11 am, Woods

line: An Oklahoma Cherokee songwriter of clear, plain songs, Americana-nominated.
intro: Ken Pomeroy has been playing shows in Oklahoma since 2016, a Cherokee songwriter with a clear, plain voice.
story: Rounder Records released her album Cruel Joke in May 2025, and she played Newport Folk that summer. In 2026 she played Pickathon on a Thursday night at Cherry Hill and a Friday afternoon in the Lucky Barn; in August she put out Tonight's News, six covers that include songs by John Denver and Woody Guthrie. That fall the Americana Music Association named her Emerging Act of the Year and put Cruel Joke up for Album of the Year. The voice hasn't changed; the audience has.
sets: Thu Jul 30, 9 pm, Cherry Hill · Fri Jul 31, 4 pm, Lucky Barn

line: A Portland songwriter, on the farm in 2026 a year after her debut, Lucky Penny.
intro: Kendall Lujan is a Portland songwriter who put out her debut, Lucky Penny, in February 2025.
story: She played Pickathon three times on one Friday in 2026, from the Lucky Barn at noon to the Farmhouse that evening, and in September released a single, "I Wonder," on ROLA Records while she shaped a second album.
sets: Fri Jul 31, noon, Lucky Barn · Fri Jul 31, 3 pm, Pumphouse · Fri Jul 31, 6 pm, Farmhouse

line: A Portland storyteller in the Prine and Welch mold, on the farm in 2026.
intro: Kyle Glenn has been telling stories in songs around Portland since 2014, in the line of John Prine and Gillian Welch.
story: In 2026 he played the Farmhouse at Pickathon on Thursday afternoon. Otherwise, look for him in the small rooms and breweries of Portland and Vancouver, Washington, where he still plays most weeks.

line: A Los Angeles power trio with a western edge, on the farm in 2026.
intro: Leroy From The North is a Los Angeles power trio with a western edge.
story: They put out Toughen Up in 2023 and a looser, wider second album, My Favorite Gun, in January 2026. That summer they played Pickathon three times, including a 1 a.m. set in the Galaxy Barn.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 9 pm, Edge · Fri Jul 31, late night (1 am), Galaxy Barn · Sat Aug 1, 3 pm, Woods

line: A Portland songwriter who also performs as Lisa Jeanne, with the Songwriters Guild in 2026.
intro: Lisa Fitzgerald is a Portland songwriter who also performs as Lisa Jeanne.
story: She has been playing out since 2022, mostly in the city's songwriter circles, and in 2026 she came to Pickathon with the Portland Songwriters Guild for a Thursday set at the Farmhouse.
sets: Thu Jul 30, 5 pm, Farmhouse

line: Storytelling songs from South Carolina's sea islands, on the farm in 2026.
intro: Lynna Corinne brings Deep South storytelling from the sea islands of South Carolina.
story: She began playing out in 2025, turned up at Portland's Dolly Parton Hoot Night, and in 2026 played a Saturday afternoon set at Pickathon's Farmhouse.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 3 pm, Farmhouse

line: A college-radio kid who helped build Bay Area indie rap. Thirty years on, still on the road.
intro: Tom Shimura came to America from Tokyo at three and found hip-hop in the cramped studios of a college radio station. Thirty years later, he was still making records the way he started: on his own terms, with his friends.
story:
Shimura grew up between Berkeley and Salt Lake City, the son of a Japanese father and an Italian mother, just as rap was arriving in the early 1980s. At UC Davis he found his people at KDVS: DJ Shadow, Gift of Gab, Chief Xcel and Lateef. When the labels said no, they made records anyway, on a label of their own, Solesides, and in 1993 its first release carried his song "Send Them." He was rapping as Asia Born then. Two years later he dropped the name; he wanted people to hear the rhymes before they judged where he came from.

The bet paid off slowly, then all at once. Latyrx, his duo with Lateef, made Robert Christgau's list of the best records of 1997. His solo debut, Later That Day, came out in 2003 on Quannum Projects, the label Solesides had grown into, and it made his name: Rolling Stone later counted it among the 200 greatest hip-hop albums ever made. The kid the industry had passed on became the first Asian-American solo rapper to play Lollapalooza, Coachella and Outside Lands.

After the big stages, he went back to clubs of a few hundred and to his own label, Mobile Home Recordings, and kept making records Christgau kept putting on his year-end lists: Quite a Life in 2018, Vision Board in 2022. In 2021 he lost Gift of Gab, the friend from those radio days who had been on nearly every album he made. Three years later he put out Goodbye, Sticky Rice. In the summer of 2026 he played Pickathon three times in one weekend, then spent the winter on the road with The Grouch, Eligh and Brother Ali. Thirty-five years after KDVS, still the same voice, still in rooms small enough to see his face.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 11 pm, Galaxy Barn · Sun Aug 2, 3 pm, Pumphouse · Sun Aug 2, 9 pm, Cherry Hill

line: A Portland band of dreamy, Fleetwood Mac-style harmonies.

line: Six decades of Brazilian bossa nova and MPB behind him in 2026.
intro: Marcos Valle was barely twenty when he and his brother wrote "Samba de Verão." The world learned it as "Summer Samba," and he has spent the sixty years since refusing to stand still.
story:
He made his first record in Rio in 1963, part of the generation that came right after bossa nova's founders, and "Samba de Verão" made him famous far beyond Brazil. In the 1970s he moved sideways, into soul, funk and electric records like Vento Sul and Previsão do Tempo, the kind of albums collectors would hunt for decades.

The rest of the world kept catching up. Estática, in 2010, won Mojo's praise as an exceptional slice of modern Rio. In 2020 he made a record for Adrian Younge and Ali Shaheed Muhammad's Jazz Is Dead series, and in 2024 Túnel Acústico came out on London's Far Out Recordings. Tum Tum Tum followed in June 2026, and that summer he headlined a Jazz Is Dead night in Solana Beach and played a Saturday night set on Pickathon's Paddock, while those 1970s albums came back out on vinyl. Past eighty, still writing summer songs.
sets: Sat Aug 1, 8 pm, Paddock

line: A MacArthur Fellow, one of jazz's most praised guitarists. About Ghosts made year-end lists.
intro: Mary Halvorson picked up the guitar because of Jimi Hendrix and learned to bend it out of shape from Anthony Braxton.
story:
She studied with Braxton at Wesleyan, moved to New York and put out her first record in 2005, and her sound was hers from the start: clean jazz lines that suddenly warp and slide, as if the tape had stretched. The prizes followed. DownBeat's critics named her best guitarist three years running, from 2017 to 2019, and in 2019 she was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship.

She kept writing for bigger groups. Belladonna and Amaryllis, a pair of 2022 records on Nonesuch, set her guitar against a string quartet and a sextet; About Ghosts followed in 2025 and made year-end lists from NPR to The Quietus, the same year Amaryllis was named DownBeat's group of the year and she was its guitarist of the year again. In 2026 she played Pickathon twice, Cherry Hill on a Friday evening and the Woods on Sunday, and that fall she took her quartet to Europe's jazz festivals. Hendrix's sound, run through Braxton's mind, still bending.
sets: Fri Jul 31, 7 pm, Cherry Hill · Sun Aug 2, 5 pm, Woods

line: Third time here, eleven years after the first, with Flora Ocean Tiger Bloom behind them.
intro: Chad Ubovich spent his early twenties playing bass in his friends' bands, Mikal Cronin's and Ty Segall's Fuzz among them. Meatbodies was where he got loud on his own.
story:
He started the band in Los Angeles in 2011, and a cassette on Segall's God? Records sold through its first run. In the Red Records put out the self-titled debut in 2014, with Segall playing on it, and Stereogum made them a Band to Watch. Alice followed in 2017.

Then a long wait. Flora Ocean Tiger Bloom took seven years and arrived in March 2024, and Pitchfork heard it as proof that psych rock was far from finished. The Portland Mercury still remembers their 2017 Pickathon set, and in 2026 they came back for a third time, eleven years after the first, with a Thursday at the Slab and a set that night at Cherry Hill. His friends taught him; his own band is still the loudest.

line: Three years on, Eblis Álvarez came back with two bands and one strange new record.
intro: Eblis Álvarez has spent nearly thirty years taking Colombian dance music apart in Bogotá and putting it back together wrong, on purpose.
story:
Meridian Brothers began in 1998 as his home-recording project, a place to bend cumbia, salsa and vallenato into strange new shapes. The London label Soundway released his albums through the 2010s, Gilles Peterson put "Guarancha UFO" on his best-of list for 2012, and the next year the band played Roskilde. Cumbia Siglo XXI came in 2020, and in 2022 an album with El Grupo Renacimiento, an old salsa band he invented and then became. In 2023 he played Big Ears and NPR's Tiny Desk.

Three years after his first visit, he came back to Pickathon in 2026 with two projects: a set with Mexican Institute of Sound early on Sunday evening, his partners on that May's album Ruido Tovar, and Meridian Brothers in the Galaxy Barn at 1 a.m. Nothing in Colombian music is safe from him yet.

story: Ruido Tovar came out on Ansonia in May 2026, Meridian Brothers' warped Colombian dance music meeting Mexican Institute of Sound's electronic cumbia. intro: Camilo Lara spent his days as an executive at EMI in Mexico City and his nights cutting old Mexican records into new music.
story:
Mexican Institute of Sound started as that side project, electronic cumbia built from samples, and its first album came out on Nacional Records in 2006. Within four years he was playing Coachella, Bonnaroo, Lollapalooza and Roskilde, and the guest list grew to include Tom Tom Club, Sly and Robbie and Toots Hibbert. His music turned up on the Grand Theft Auto V soundtrack, and in 2021 he was one of the artists remaking Metallica's songs for The Metallica Blacklist.

In 2026 he remixed the World Cup theme for Mexico, released Ruido Tovar with Meridian Brothers in May, and played a Friday night set on Pickathon's Paddock. The side project long ago became the main event.

In 2023 he formed Setting with Jaime Fennelly and Joe Westerlund. Eleven years after a Lucky Barn session on his first visit, he came back to Pickathon in 2026 for a Sunday afternoon alone at the Windmill, and two more sets with Setting. The old instrument, still going somewhere new.

story: Her early albums came out on small labels, and she toured the way island musicians do, a long way from anywhere. In 2019 a car crash broke both of Weiss's legs. Four years later Quasi came back with Breaking the Balls of History on Sub Pop, their first album in a decade, and Mojo called it their "most corrosive cocktail yet"; in 2024 they toured their 1998 album Featuring Birds in full. In 2026 they played Pickathon three times, from the Slab on Saturday to a Sunday evening in the Woods. The marriage ended; the band never did.

line: Americana's emerging act of 2015, back in 2026 as a headliner with a fifth album.
intro: Alejandro Rose-Garcia started Shakey Graves as one man with a guitar and an old suitcase he kicked like a bass drum. Fifteen years and a gold record later, his newest album sounds almost that close.

In Austin he made the one-man band his calling card, self-releasing his first album in 2011 and building an audience one show at a time. And the War Came, in October 2014, reached No. 44 on the Billboard 200, and "Dearly Departed," his duet with Esmé Patterson, went gold. Conan, Letterman and Seth Meyers followed, then an NPR Tiny Desk, and in 2015 the Americana Music Association named him its Emerging Act of the Year.

The band grew and so did the records: Can't Wake Up in 2018, Movie of the Week in 2023, and "Ready or Not," a duet with Sierra Ferrell that climbed to No. 15 on the AAA chart. Then, in May 2026, Fondness, Etc., quiet and lo-fi. That summer took him from Telluride Bluegrass to London's Islington Assembly Hall, and to his fourth Pickathon, with two sets at the Slab, a Friday night on the Paddock and Saturday night in the Woods. The suitcase days are not so far behind him.

line: Three Grammys and some twenty nominations behind him when he came in 2026.
intro: Steve Earle was a teenager in Texas when Townes Van Zandt became his teacher. Half a century later, other songwriters learn from him.
story:
He went to Nashville in 1974 and wrote for other singers for a decade before Guitar Town, in 1986, made him a star and earned two Grammy nominations. Then addiction took most of the early '90s from him.

He came back writing harder than ever. Train a Comin', in 1995, started a run of records nominated for the Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk Album; The Revolution Starts... Now won it, then Washington Square Serenade, then Townes, his album of his teacher's songs, in 2010. He made a bluegrass record, The Mountain, with the Del McCoury Band, acted in The Wire and Treme, and in 2020 the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame took him in.

That same year his son, Justin Townes Earle, died. J.T., an album of Justin's songs, came out in the first days of 2021, and the Americana Music Association put it up for Album of the Year. In 2025 the Grand Ole Opry made him a member, and in 2026 he went out alone on a tour called 51 Years of Songs and Stories, playing Pickathon's Paddock on Saturday night and the Woods on Sunday before a run through Europe with The Waterboys. The student Townes taught is the teacher now.

Daptone signed them and released a run of 1960s-style singles, and they opened for Thee Sacred Souls and LA LOM. At Pickathon that summer they played three sets, and Portland Monthly called the last of them, Sunday night on the Woods Stage, "transcendent." Less than two weeks later their self-titled debut came out on Daptone, and that same day they played the Hollywood Bowl with Al Green; Mojo and Uncut both put it on their lists of the year's best. Sam Cooke's granddaughters, writing their own chapter.
